national_articles.headline: Brigade Group to invest Rs 40,000 crore in 3 years, build 40 million sq ft across South India
national_articles.body: Realty firm Brigade Group on Thursday said it will invest Rs 40,000 crore over the next three years to develop housing, commercial, hospitality and warehousing projects across major cities in South India, as part of its expansion plan. Bengaluru-based Brigade Group on Thursday marked the completion of 40 years in business. Outlining its growth plans for the next three years, Brigade Group said in a statement that it will invest around Rs 40,000 crores over the next three years for a development pipeline of 40 million sq. ft. across its markets. Over the past four decades, Brigade has developed more than 110 million sq. ft. across 300+ projects and established its presence across 10 cities. The Group has built a diversified portfolio that includes residential communities, office developments, retail destinations, and hotels. "Brigade was built on the belief that real estate is ultimately about creating places that have enduring value for people, businesses and communities. Over four decades, we have grown with the cities and markets in which we operate, adapting to changing aspirations and economic realities," M R Jaishankar, Executive Chairman, Brigade Group, said.  The next phase will be about taking that experience into new markets and new opportunities, he added.

national_articles.headline: India confident of hitting $1 trillion in exports this fiscal despite global headwinds: Piyush Goyal
national_articles.body: Market Mastery Find the weak links India is on track to meet its $1-trillion exports target this financial year despite a challenging global economic environment, commerce and industry Minister Piyush Goyal said on October 8. Speaking at an event organised by the Confederation of Indian Industry, Goyal said India has set a target of about 16 percent growth in exports at $1 trillion, even as global trade is expected to grow by only 2.5-3 percent. “I am confident, looking at half-year numbers, that we will achieve this,” Goyal said. During April-August, goods and services exports jumped 25 percent on-year to $82.68 billion, while services exports were estimated at $38.87 billion, generating a services trade surplus of $17.45 billion. This brought the overall goods and services trade deficit down to $9.41 billion. India recorded exports worth $863 billion last year, Goyal said, adding the country was seeking a significant increase in exports at a time when the global economy remains vulnerable to shocks. Goyal attributed India's resilience to the contribution of businesses, including the country's 63 million MSMEs, global capability centres, emerging technology companies and around 250,000 startups. India was increasingly engaging with global markets from a position of confidence and had the ability to compete with the world, the minister said. Goyal urged the CII to set up free trade agreement (FTA)  utilisation desks across in state councils to help MSMEs make better use of these agreements. These desks should help businesses identify new market opportunities, understand rules of origin and participate in trade delegations, he said. India's FTAs protect sensitive sectors, particularly MSMEs, agriculture and fishermen, while opening up opportunities for exports of agricultural and marine products as well as high-precision engineering goods, the minister said. India is also confident of growing at over 7 percent this fiscal. Referring to the Reserve Bank of India's upward revision to its growth forecast, he said India would continue to remain the world's fastest-growing large economy despite global challenges. The central bank on October 7 raised its full-year real GDP growth forecast for FY27 to 7.1 percent from its earlier projection of 6.7 percent, the latest in a string of upgrades over the last month. Goyal said the government had prioritised structural reforms and technology adoption, citing the implementation of GST and the digital India programme. He said Prime Minister Narendra Modi had earlier highlighted that digital India had resulted in savings of more than Rs 5 lakh crore, or over $55 billion, for the country over the past 12 years. Goyal also said India was embracing new technologies rather than viewing them as a threat to jobs, arguing that advances in technology would create new opportunities for the country's young workforce. “Trust is a scarce commodity in the world today but India is that rare oasis which is a trusted partner,” Goyal said. The country was increasingly willing to adopt and engage with exacting global standards as it seeks to expand its presence in international markets. The government and industry were working together towards the broader goal of making India a developed nation by 2047, he said.

national_articles.headline: Indian firms seen posting faster profit growth despite global headwinds
national_articles.body: Indian companies' September-quarter profit growth is expected to accelerate even as performance is likely to be uneven across sectors due to global and local headwinds, according to five brokerages. Foreign investors have pulled out of Indian stocks at a record pace, pushing the benchmark Nifty 50 towards its worst year in 15 years. While a weakest-in-a-decade monsoon has raised rural demand concerns, the Middle East conflict has fuelled inflation concerns globally, raising the risk premium on emerging market economies and equity markets. However, "resilient domestic demand in Q2, early festive inventory build-up, favourable pricing in selective commodity-linked sectors should continue to support earnings growth," said J.P.Morgan analysts led by Rajiv Batra. Nifty 50 firms' net profit is forecast to rise about 20% year-on-year on average, based on brokerage estimates. In April-June, it hit a 10-quarter high of 18% following three quarters of low-single-digit growth. Motilal Oswal is the most optimistic, forecasting a 27% increase in net profit, which would be the fastest in 17 quarters. The broker is bullish on automobiles and new-age tech platforms, picking the likes of Meesho, PhysicsWallah, Mahindra & Mahindra and TVS Motor, on structural growth trends, recovering discretionary demand and expanding product portfolios. PhillipCapital expects a modest 13% rise, reflecting margin pressure and a less favourable mix outside the oil and gas sector. Tata Consultancy Services will kickstart the earnings season later in the day.  Most analysts back financials to be the principal earnings anchor, with healthy loan growth, lower credit costs and fewerloansturning bad at banks. "Following the Reserve Bank of India's rate hike and its shift to a 'calibrated tightening' stance, we expect large private banks to see further earnings upgrades," said J.P.Morgan. Multiple brokerages say earnings from ICICI Bank, State Bank of India and Bajaj Finance would stand out. Effects of the US-Iran war, now in its eighth month, are likely to be felt sharply across automobiles, energy and consumer goods, as oil from the region struggled to get through to India, the world's third-largest crude importer, raising costs. Automobile retail sales rose during the quarter on improved product mix, pricing and tax cuts. However, Kotak Institutional Equities expects commodity headwinds to drag operating margins. Higher crude prices are likely to favour upstream and oil-to-chemicals companies, while pressuring oil marketing firms. Oil-to-telecom conglomerate and operator of the world's largest refining complex, Reliance Industries, is expected to benefit from this, tiding over a relatively softer retail performance. IT demand may remain subdued as clients delay non-essential spending amid AI-driven pricing pressure.  "We expect management commentaries to reflect the multi-pronged challenges the sector faces — geopolitics, weak macro and AI threat," Nuvama said.

national_articles.headline: NCLT clears its highest ever 107 resolution plans in Q2 despite 14 vacancies, 4 more members due to retire by year-end
national_articles.body: Market Mastery Find the weak links The National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) approved 107 resolution plans in the July-September quarter of 2026-27, its highest quarterly performance since its inception, even as the tribunal continues to function with 14 vacancies and a substantial number of courts operating only for half a day. The plans approved during the second quarter carried a combined value of Rs 11,071.17 crore, according to data released by the NCLT on Wednesday (October 7). The latest performance takes the number of resolution plans approved during the first half of FY2026-27 to 185 and the cumulative tally across NCLT benches to 1,735 as of September 30. Q2 approvals cross previous high The 107 approvals in Q2 are substantially higher than the corresponding figures of previous years. The NCLT approved 60 resolution plans in the second quarter of FY2025-26, 57 in FY2024-25, 82 in FY2023-24, 47 in FY2022-23 and 20 in FY2021-22. The tribunal had approved 78 plans in the first quarter of the current financial year. Thus, 185 plans were approved between April and September 2026. The cumulative figure of 1,735 includes 19 approvals in FY2017-18, 81 in FY2018-19, 142 in FY2019-20, 122 in FY2020-21, 157 in FY2021-22, 208 in FY2022-23, 276 in FY2023-24, 288 in FY2024-25 and 257 in FY2025-26. The cumulative approved amount across these years stands at Rs 4,89,292 crore, with the 185 plans approved in the first half of FY2026-27 accounting for ₹16,588 crore. Mumbai leads, but plan count does not tell whole story Mumbai recorded the highest number of approvals during the second quarter, clearing 35 resolution plans. The Principal and New Delhi Benches followed with 29, while Chandigarh approved nine and Ahmedabad eight. Indore cleared six plans, Kolkata five, and Allahabad, Bengaluru and Hyderabad four each. Chennai, Guwahati and Jaipur approved one plan apiece. The value of plans also varied sharply between benches. Mumbai's 35 approvals were valued at Rs 4,189.47 crore, while the Principal and New Delhi Benches approved 29 plans worth Rs 1,648.74 crore. Ahmedabad's eight plans were worth Rs 288.22 crore, Chandigarh's nine amounted to Rs 107.91 crore and Indore's six plans were valued at Rs 106.66 crore. Jaipur, despite approving only one plan, recorded an approved value of Rs 288.37 crore. Kolkata's five plans, by comparison, were valued at Rs 27.28 crore. The NCLT's bench-wise data shows that the number of plans cleared by a bench did not necessarily correspond to their aggregate monetary value. Pendency remains an issue The record disposal came against the backdrop of continuing applications seeking approval of resolution plans. The Supreme Court had noted on April 29 that 363 applications were awaiting approval before the NCLT. By September 30, 294 resolution plans were pending consideration, while orders had been reserved in another 41 matters. This meant 335 matters were at either of these two stages, a reduction from the position recorded by the Supreme Court in April. The NCLT said it has strengthened its monitoring of pendency and disposal across its 16 Benches, allowing it to track workload and redistribute cases where necessary. It has also introduced a framework for registration and listing of cases, developed after consultations with the Bar. The system prioritises older matters, including IBC admission cases and applications for approval of resolution plans. The tribunal has additionally undertaken workload redistribution and constituted Special Benches wherever required. 14 vacancies, more expected by year-end The performance has been recorded despite the tribunal operating below its sanctioned strength. Against 62 sanctioned Members, apart from the President, the NCLT currently has 48 working Members, leaving 14 vacancies. Four more Members are due to demit office by the end of the calendar year. The shortage has affected the functioning of the courts. According to the tribunal, 13 Courts are presently operating on a full-day basis, while 18 function on a half-day basis. "The shortage of members has an impact on the functioning of Courts, with 13 Courts presently functioning on a full-day basis and 18 Courts functioning on a half-day basis. Further, 4 more Members are due to demit office by the end of the current calendar year," the statement said. The NCLT has also indicated that increasing its sanctioned strength could enable it to consider dedicated Special Benches for real estate resolution plans. Members also advocated pre-mediation as a way of reducing pendency. Digital push alongside case management The tribunal has introduced e-Inspection and e-Certified Copy services to provide advocates, litigants and other stakeholders faster access to judicial records and certified copies. These initiatives form part of its wider digital transition, alongside the revamped NCLT website and implementation of e-Courts 2.0. The NCLT's institutional capacity has also come under Supreme Court scrutiny. The apex court has taken suo motu cognizance of issues concerning appointments of Judicial and Technical Members and inadequate infrastructure, and directed the Union government to submit a status report on basic amenities at the Principal and Regional Benches.  Against this backdrop, the NCLT said it would continue focusing on timely disposal, efficient case management and better utilisation of its available judicial and administrative resources.

international_articles.headline: 'Both of y'all want a f** piece of me': Bodycam captures 6-year-old after teacher shooting
international_articles.body: Market Mastery Find the weak links Newly released body-camera footage has shed light on the moments after a six-year-old boy shot his first-grade teacher inside a classroom at Richneck Elementary School in Newport News, Virginia, in January 2023. The footage, which was recently unsealed by a court, shows police officers entering the classroom after Abby Zwerner was shot. The boy, identified in court documents only as JT, was being restrained by reading specialist Amy Kovac when officers arrived. The child can be heard repeatedly using profanity while speaking to Kovac and the officers. At one point, he tells the officers, “Both y'all want a f*** piece of me, b**h?!” Zwerner was shot on January 6, 2023, in front of 16 students. The bullet went through her hand before lodging in her chest. She suffered life-threatening injuries but survived. No students were injured. A 9mm Taurus handgun can be seen lying on the classroom floor a few feet from the boy. Kovac tells officers that the weapon is there and that the child had admitted to having it. “The gun is there,” she said. “He just admitted he had one. … bullet.” Officers subsequently locate the firearm. Kovac also tells them that she had previously warned Assistant Principal Ebony Parker about a threat involving the child. “I told the AP [Parker] that there was a threat earlier…” Kovac said. The teacher tells the officers that the boy is six years old, attends school on a modified schedule and that it was his first week attending without his mother accompanying him. Kovac had called 911 after hearing the gunshot and then went to the classroom, where she held the child in a bear hug. Officers ask the boy whether he is hurt. He responds that he is not. Kovac then checks his hands and later tells police that she can see gunshot residue on them. When officers ask where the weapon is, the boy points toward it. “It’s over there, [expletive],” the boy said. Kovac tells him to stop using profanity, but the child responds with further abuse. “[Expletive] you,” the boy said. KOVAC: “That’s not how we speak to each other. “[Expletive] you, [expletive],” the boy said. The footage later captures the child explaining how he got the firearm. “My mom had that. I stole that from my mom,” the boy said. “I don’t care if you call backup. I don’t care if I go to jail.” At another point, the child tells someone, “If you want a piece of me, come get it.” The approximately three-minute footage ends as officers take the boy out of the classroom. He appears to strike Kovac before police escort him away. According to the footage, the handgun was jammed and had seven rounds remaining. The video was released as part of legal proceedings stemming from the shooting. The Virginian-Pilot and Daily Press had sought to have the body-camera footage unsealed, and a judge later approved its release with conditions to protect the child's identity, including blurring his face. The footage was also used in Zwerner's civil lawsuit against former assistant principal Ebony Parker. Zwerner alleged that Parker failed to act after being warned about the child having a gun. Zwerner was awarded $10 million in the civil case against Parker last year. A separate criminal case against Parker was dismissed earlier this year.  The newly unsealed footage offers a detailed account of the immediate police response, the recovery of the firearm and the child's statements about how he obtained the weapon from his mother.

international_articles.headline: US midterms on track to break spending records as billionaires and corporations pour in money
international_articles.body: The 2026 US midterm elections are shaping up to be among the most expensive ever, with billionaires, corporations, political parties and special-interest groups pouring extraordinary sums into congressional and state races. The elections are on course to break spending records, according to the Brennan Center for Justice. Yet there is a striking twist, as reported by the Washington Post: all that money is not necessarily producing the results donors want. Republicans have spent about half a billion dollars in recent weeks, but the spending has so far failed to shift polls decisively in their favour. Dark money has already crossed USD1 billion One of the biggest features of this election is the amount of money flowing through organisations that do not have to reveal their donors. At least USD1 billion in such “dark money” was spent during the primaries alone, according to a New York Times analysis cited by The Washington Post. Dark-money spending expanded after the 2010 Citizens United Supreme Court decision allowed corporations to spend unlimited amounts on politics. Technology interests are another major source of campaign money. Artificial intelligence and cryptocurrency groups have spent more than USD100 million in the primaries and are prepared to spend heavily against candidates who oppose their positions. Some candidates are even trying to distance themselves from outside spending. In Michigan, Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers asked the pro-Israel American Israel Public Affairs Committee not to spend on his race. Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, meanwhile, won his primary after making the group's spending for his opponent an issue in his campaign. Republicans have a major financial advantage Political parties have greater freedom to spend this year following a Supreme Court decision that allowed them to spend unlimited amounts in coordination with candidates, removing previous restrictions. Republicans have raised substantially more than Democrats, while President Donald Trump has begun using hundreds of millions of dollars from his political war chest to support Republican candidates. But money has not automatically translated into stronger polling. Despite Republicans putting roughly USD500 million into races over recent weeks, The Post reported that polls have not moved significantly in their favour. In some Senate contests, Democratic candidates have actually become more popular during the spending blitz. Texas has become a spending battleground Few races illustrate the scale of spending better than the Texas Senate contest between Republican Ken Paxton and Democrat James Talarico. Republican spending to support Paxton has reached levels comparable with presidential campaign spending in Texas. Talarico, however, has tried to turn the flood of money against his opponent into a campaign argument, linking wealthy political donors to voters' concerns about affordability and economic inequality. Polls cited by The Post show the race remains extremely close. Can too much campaign money backfire? Campaign money still matters enormously. It allows candidates to dominate television, digital and other media with advertising, increase their name recognition and shape how voters perceive them. It can also finance efforts to persuade supporters to turn out and vote. But there may be a point at which additional spending becomes less effective. In Ohio's governor's race, Republican nominee Vivek Ramaswamy has spent millions attacking Democrat Amy Acton, but analysts have warned that relentless negative campaigning from both sides could simply cause voters to tune out. Elon Musk offers another example. After spending hundreds of millions of dollars to help Trump return to the White House, his super PAC is now spending tens of millions to support Republican Senate candidates. Democrats, however, are hoping Musk's national unpopularity will help motivate their own voters and donors. Musk previously spent USD13 million on a Wisconsin Supreme Court race, where the candidate he supported lost. The tension is summed up by government ethics expert Meredith McGehee: having enormous amounts of money does not guarantee victory, but having too little can make defeat much more likely.  The public debate over campaign finance may also be spreading beyond individual races. Voters in Republican-leaning Montana will decide whether their state should become the first in the country to ban corporations from spending money on elections.

international_articles.headline: US military rethinks Middle East presence after Iranian attacks damage key bases
international_articles.body: The United States is moving military forces away from bases in the Middle East and Britain as the war with Iran exposes vulnerabilities that were not anticipated when US President Donald Trump ordered the attack on Iran in February. The latest move came over the weekend, when the US hurriedly withdrew 12 B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford in Britain. Trump described the decision as a precaution, while US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the Pentagon routinely moves military resources according to where they are needed. American and British officials, however, said commanders had received specific and credible intelligence that Iran-backed operatives were planning drone attacks against the aircraft and US personnel from just outside the base. According to the New York Times, the withdrawal follows the evacuation of American personnel from bases in Bahrain, Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates and Qatar after Iranian attacks. Some bases have been so badly damaged that the Pentagon has little interest in rebuilding them in their existing locations, according to the report. Drones have changed calculations about military bases The suspected threat against RAF Fairford highlights a problem extending well beyond the Middle East. Military forces traditionally sought protection by positioning themselves beyond the range of an adversary's weapons. But relatively inexpensive drones can now be transported close to a target and launched locally, making distance less useful as a defence. The suspected plotters in Britain may have been partly inspired by Ukraine's attack inside Russia last year, when drones were smuggled deep into the country and launched from trucks, damaging or destroying at least a dozen aircraft. Such attacks, along with the growing importance of cyberweapons, have forced the Pentagon to reconsider how vulnerable its overseas bases may be. Iranian attacks have damaged US bases across the Gulf When Trump announced the attack on Iran on February 28, he initially expected the conflict to produce a victory within days and later within five or six weeks. Three weeks into the fighting, he declared Iran totally defeated. Instead, Iran retaliated against American bases throughout the Middle East. Many of the 13 principal bases used by US forces in the region were quickly rendered uninhabitable, with facilities in Kuwait suffering particularly severe damage. American troops were moved into hotels and office buildings, but Iran subsequently identified some of those locations and began targeting them as well. Six US service members were killed when a strike on Port Shuaiba destroyed an Army tactical operations centre. Iranian drones and missiles also struck Ali Al Salem Air Base and Camp Buehring in Kuwait. In Qatar, an attack on Al Udeid Air Base, the regional air headquarters of US Central Command, damaged an early-warning radar system. Iranian attacks also damaged communications equipment at the headquarters of the US Fifth Fleet in Bahrain and hit communications equipment and refuelling tankers at Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia. US military operations are becoming more complicated The relocations do not prevent the United States from conducting military operations, but they make them more difficult and expensive. American bombers can still strike targets from bases in the United States, but the longer journeys require additional time and aerial refuelling. Aircraft carriers can operate in the Arabian Sea, but they must now be supplied from Diego Garcia in the Indian Ocean, about 2,200 miles away, adding weeks and substantial costs to logistics. The United States has also been unable to guarantee freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and parts of the Red Sea, despite protection of these shipping routes having long been a central justification for the American military presence in the region. Trump administration says the pressure on Iran is working The administration presents a different assessment of the war's progress. Trump has argued that Iran is approaching economic collapse and says the naval blockade, which has reduced its oil exports to a trickle, will eventually force Tehran into an agreement. Administration officials also describe the base evacuations as prudent and temporary rather than evidence of a broader retreat. The Pentagon is nevertheless considering a significant reorganisation of its presence in the Middle East. Officials are examining possible new bases in Israel and Jordan, although these would require congressional approval and could take years to build or upgrade.  US Central Command is also conducting serious planning over how its facilities across the region should be repositioned and reshaped, as the financial costs of the war and of repairing damaged bases continue to rise.

international_articles.headline: Meet Jonathan, the 194-year-old tortoise who could hold clues to longer life
international_articles.body: At about 194 years old, Jonathan has lived through almost two centuries of human history. Now scientists have sequenced the giant tortoise’s genome for the first time, hoping his DNA could provide clues about how some animals manage to live for such extraordinary lengths of time. Jonathan is the world’s oldest known land animal. The Aldabra giant tortoise lives on the remote island of St. Helena, around 1,200 miles off Africa’s west coast, where he spends his days on the grounds of the governor’s official residence. He is believed to have been born around 1832. His keepers estimate that he was already at least 50 when he arrived on St. Helena, based on his size at the time. Despite his age, Jonathan remains remarkably active. Cataracts have left him mostly blind, but his hearing is still excellent and he retains a strong libido. He enjoys visitors, likes having his neck stroked and is known for producing loud belches when crowds gather around his paddock at feeding time. Getting Jonathan’s DNA was not easy According to the New York Times, Jonathan’s age offered scientists something extremely unusual: an opportunity to examine the genome of an animal that has lived for nearly 200 years while it is still alive. But obtaining a usable sample presented problems. Researchers were not permitted to draw blood because of the infection risk, so veterinarian Joe Hollins instead had to take a swab from inside Jonathan’s cheek. That was not particularly straightforward either. Jonathan weighs around 400 pounds, has a razor-sharp beak and gave Hollins only a few seconds to collect the sample before he risked being struck by one of the tortoise’s powerful legs. The first attempt produced a swab covered in half-chewed carrot. Once collected, the saliva sample faced another complication. St. Helena has only one commercial flight a week, which is frequently delayed, so Jonathan’s DNA eventually had to make part of its journey by boat. What scientists found in his genome After sequencing the DNA, researchers compared Jonathan’s genome with those of tortoises about 100 years younger. They found molecular differences, particularly in genes associated with DNA repair and with maintaining telomeres, the protective structures at the ends of chromosomes. Both processes are closely connected with aging. DNA gradually accumulates damage as organisms grow older, while telomeres become shorter. Jonathan’s genome suggests that Aldabra giant tortoises may have evolved mechanisms that make them more resilient to some forms of age-related decline, although researchers say considerably more testing is required. Scientists also found that Jonathan shares some genes with other exceptionally long-lived animals, including naked mole rats, which can live for around 40 years and rarely develop cancer. One part of Jonathan still looks surprisingly young Some of the most intriguing findings came not from Jonathan’s genome itself but from his epigenome, the chemical markers that help control when genes are switched on and off. As expected for an animal of his age, Jonathan showed many epigenetic changes similar to those seen in elderly humans. But one area stood out. The regulatory switches associated with his mitochondria were unusually well preserved and resembled those of a young tortoise. Mitochondria provide energy to cells and have long been associated with healthy aging. That does not mean Jonathan holds a simple secret to human longevity. Researchers caution that he is a single animal and may simply be exceptional. His unusually long life could also have been helped by his circumstances: he receives constant veterinary attention, eats fresh vegetables and lives in the protected grounds of the governor’s residence. Scientists therefore want to study many more Aldabra giant tortoises and other long-lived animals before drawing broader conclusions.  As study lead author Stephen Clark put it, understanding Jonathan would be considerably easier if scientists had 1,000 animals like him. For now, the nearly two-century-old tortoise offers a rare glimpse into what extreme longevity looks like at the molecular level.
